question: What does each blockchain network, DeFi protocol and yield product control, where can it stop a payment, and how does it make money?
answer: Very different amounts. On Ethereum, validators can censor or leave out transactions; on Stellar and Hedera each token's issuer sets its own freeze controls. Aave, Sky and Curve can change settings, caps or fees by governance vote, but Liquity's core design has no way to pause, upgrade or blacklist. Ethena and Ondo control who may mint and redeem; Morpho's governance cannot pause existing markets, while its vault curators choose where lenders' money goes. They earn from network fees, borrowing interest and protocol fees, and Ethena from derivatives funding payments.

items.label: On this page
items.note: Of the 22 cards in the library's company control map.

sections.title: One by one
sections.sub: Each card opens to all 14 fields: what it owns, where it can say no, how it makes money, its legal entities and how it can break.

items.title: Ethereum ecosystem
items.sub: live · several independent software clients · community-governed
items.text: Ethereum hosts stablecoins and other financial tokens but is not their issuer
kv: Owns

No single body owns Ethereum. The Ethereum Foundation, software client teams, validators, node operators, standards authors, infrastructure firms and layer-2 (L2) network operators have different roles.
Can say no
Validators can censor transactions or leave them out. Client teams and the community can choose software and recovery plans. Application admins keep their own keys.
Makes money from
ETH fees and burn, validator rewards and MEV (profit from ordering transactions), L2 income, RPC and wallet services, and application fees.
Sits on
Running and settling transactions, smart-contract records and apps that plug into each other
Legal entities

The Ethereum Foundation is a Swiss Stiftung (foundation) and an influential funder and organizer. It is not the protocol, the validators or an issuer. Consensys Software Inc. runs products such as MetaMask and Infura and contributes client software, but it does not own Ethereum.
Money products
ETH pays transaction fees (gas) and secures consensus. USDC, PYUSD, USDe, GHO and tokenized securities are liabilities or claims of other systems.
Control levers
EIP (Ethereum Improvement Proposal) debate, AllCoreDevs coordination, independent client builds, node and validator adoption, rare community-led recovery, and app and L2 upgrade keys.
Depends on
Client diversity, validator concentration, RPC access, bridges and L2s, oracles (outside data feeds), app admins and stablecoin issuers.
Stablecoin and DeFi role
The main network where issuer coins, lending, decentralized exchanges (DEXs), synthetic dollars, vaults and tokenized assets work together.
Path to shops
Usually through L2s, wallets, processors or crypto-linked cards, not direct retail use of the base layer-1 (L1) chain.
GENIUS Act
The network does not decide whether a coin is a payment stablecoin. The exact issuer and its redemption promise do.
Latest
Protocol upgrades need client teams to build them and validators and nodes to adopt them. No single company controls every layer.
Can break by
Client bug, validator concentration, finality failure, community split, L2 or bridge failure, or a compromised app admin.
Limit
The Ethereum Foundation (EF) does not own Ethereum, and Consensys does not control it. Validators do not formally vote on every EIP. Stablecoin value does not become EF revenue or liability.
open: In practice, how concentrated are clients, staking providers, RPC providers, L2 sequencers and stablecoin admins?

items.title: Stellar / SDF
items.sub: cash conversion and stablecoin payments live · DTC connection not yet live
items.text: Stellar treats reaching users, not the token, as the main constraint
kv: Owns

The Stellar Development Foundation (SDF) supports protocol development and ecosystem programs. Third-party issuers, anchors (cash-conversion companies), validators, wallets and MoneyGram keep separate roles.
Can say no

Each issuer can set authorization, freeze or clawback-style controls on its asset. Anchors can refuse conversion. Validators choose which validators they trust (quorum sets) and vote on protocol versions and settings.
Makes money from
Users need XLM for fees, rent and minimum balances. But fees go into a fee pool no one can access, and validators receive no protocol rewards. Anchors, wallets and applications earn separately.
Sits on
Moving assets cheaply, standards for anchors, converting cash, and distributing regulated assets
Legal entities
The Stellar Development Foundation is a nonprofit support body. It is not the issuer of USDC, PYUSD, MGUSD or tokenized funds.
Money products
XLM pays fees and minimum balances (reserves). Third-party stablecoins and securities keep their own legal issuers.
Control levers
Protocol releases, validator quorum choices, SDF ecosystem funding, issuer settings on each asset, anchors and wallet integrations.
Depends on
Issuers, the MoneyGram/Crossmint cash network, anchors, validators, wallets, card networks and a future DTC (Depository Trust Company) connection.
Stablecoin and DeFi role
USDC, PYUSD and locally distributed stablecoins can connect cash, remittances, aid, wallets and tokenized assets.
Path to shops
MoneyGram and wallet apps convert cash to and from stablecoins. Visa/Wirex settlement and spending through apps offer other paths.
GENIUS Act
SDF is normally infrastructure, not a payment-stablecoin issuer. Each asset on Stellar needs its own legal test.
Latest
Cash conversion and payments are live. The DTC connection targets H1 2027 (first half). The Protocol 26/CAP-77 emergency ledger-key quarantine must be confirmed on mainnet before we call it live.
Can break by
Anchor insolvency, issuer freeze, validator quorum fault, wallet failure or trading split across too many places.
Limit
SDF is not a bank or stablecoin issuer. XLM is not reserve backing. A DTC connection does not replace DTC's own books. Validators are not paid like miners or stakers.
open: How wider distribution turns into lasting income for the network and token, and how issuer controls work with Soroban smart contracts.

items.title: Hedera
items.sub: network and tools live · range of real production use still uneven
items.text: Hedera offers businesses built-in tools that let issuers control their own tokens
kv: Owns
A network whose rules and ownership the Hedera Council governs, plus ecosystem tools. Stablecoin Studio is an open-source kit that third-party issuers use to issue coins.
Can say no
The Council governs network software, treasury and pricing. Token issuers set their own keys for identity checks (KYC), freezing, pausing, wiping balances and supply.
Makes money from
Network fees paid in HBAR and ecosystem activity. Issuers and applications earn separately.
Sits on
Council-run consensus, built-in token tools, predictable fees and business workflows mixing public and private systems
Legal entities

Hedera Hashgraph, LLC dba (doing business as) Hedera Council is the Delaware entity that governs the network. Hedera Foundation and Hashgraph are independent ecosystem and software organizations. Hiero is the open-source project. All are separate from token issuers.
Money products
HBAR pays public-network fees and secures consensus. Stablecoins, tokenized collateral and state-issued tokens are claims on third parties.
Control levers

Council decisions govern treasury, pricing, membership, releases and mainnet-node policy. Only Council members currently run mainnet consensus nodes. Each token is controlled by keys its issuer sets in the Hedera Token Service (HTS): admin, supply, KYC, freeze, wipe, fee and pause.
Depends on
Council continuity, nodes, outside issuers, custodians, reserve-data providers and oracles (outside data feeds) such as Chainlink.
Stablecoin and DeFi role
Stablecoin Studio provides connection points for compliance and proof of reserves. Hedera Token Service provides built-in controls over a token's whole life.
Path to shops
Issuer and payment-provider apps can use Hedera. Merchant acceptance still runs through wallets, processors and acquirers (merchants' payment banks).
GENIUS Act
Stablecoin Studio may help an issuer meet control rules. It cannot supply the legal issuer, rights to reserves or approval.
Latest
Wyoming FRNT and commercial projects show real deployment. Institutional pilots still need confirmation that they are in production.
Can break by
Council or node concentration, stolen keys, an issuer-admin action, an oracle or custody fault, or private and public networks falling out of sync.
Limit
Open-source Hiero code does not let anyone join mainnet without approval. Council governance does not make Hedera the issuer of every token made with its tools.
open: Which uses repeat at scale, and how public Hedera connects with private HashSphere networks.

items.title: Aave
items.text: Aave DAO controls GHO by deciding who may mint it and how much
kv: Owns
No ordinary parent owns the protocol. Aave DAO (decentralized autonomous organization, run by token votes) governs deployments and GHO; Aave Labs builds software and interfaces.
Can say no
Governance can add or remove facilitators and change caps. Stewards can adjust rates, exposures and freezes within limits governance gave them.
Makes money from
Borrowing interest, protocol fees, liquidation income and GHO revenue directed to the DAO-controlled treasury.
Sits on
Collateral-backed loans, liquidity and how much GHO each approved minter (facilitator) may create
Legal entities

Aave DAO and community, Aave Labs (with its interface and trademark roles), independent risk and technical service providers, stewards and GHO facilitators are different actors. Aave Labs' terms deny that it controls the protocol.
Money products
GHO is the protocol dollar and sGHO its savings receipt. Aave also has deposit and debt tokens and the AAVE governance token.
Control levers
Governance executors, each facilitator's mint limit (bucket), guardians, stewards with limited powers, risk providers, oracle choices and Aave Labs' interface policies.
Depends on
Collateral, Chainlink and other oracles (price-data services), liquidators, governance voting, service providers and stablecoin liquidity.
Stablecoin and DeFi role
GHO is a dollar the DAO controls. Aave also provides the lending and yield underneath regulated coins.
Path to shops
Most likely a wallet or processor converts GHO, or a card service lets someone spend against an Aave or Morpho position.
GENIUS Act
Strong argument that GHO is not a payment stablecoin, since no named company owes fiat redemption. Approval for institutional use remains uncertain.
Latest
RemoteGSM (remote GHO Stability Module) and a modular design spread GHO across more chains; minting still comes only from governance-approved sources.
Can break by
An oracle or collateral shock, a takeover of governance, a facilitator fault, failed liquidations or a smart-contract exploit.
Limit
Aave Labs is not automatically the issuer or operator of every DAO deployment.
open: Whether the DAO is treated as a person or issuer, facilitators' legal liability, and processor acceptance.

items.title: Sky / Maker lineage
items.sub: DAI, USDS and sUSDS live · who the issuer is remains unresolved
items.text: Sky calls its dollars a 'protocol obligation,' but no clear legal entity owes holders
kv: Owns

Sky governance controls collateral, rates, PSMs (peg stability modules), how executive decisions are carried out, and the upgradeable USDS contracts. Ecosystem entities provide interfaces and support.
Can say no
Governance can change settings and contract code. Interfaces can restrict users. Collateral custodians keep their own controls over each asset.
Makes money from
Lending and RWA investments produce protocol income. That income pays savings rates, rewards, expenses and token buybacks.
Sits on
Which collateral is accepted, how many dollars exist, the savings rate and the move to the new protocol
Legal entities

Sky governance controls the protocol. Skybase International provides an interface and says it is not the issuer or operator. Sky Frontier Foundation, Agents such as Spark and Grove, and collateral SPVs (special purpose vehicles) and other entities are separate; do not treat them as one.
Money products
DAI and USDS are protocol dollars. sUSDS and the DSR (Dai Savings Rate) are separate savings claims. Collateral includes crypto, stablecoins and RWAs (real-world assets).
Control levers
Executive votes and the code they run (spells), token upgrades, PSMs, rates, Agents and interface terms.
Depends on
USDC and other collateral issuers, oracles, custodians, governance voting, market liquidity and front ends.
Stablecoin and DeFi role
One of the most liquid protocol-dollar and DeFi (decentralized finance) collateral systems. USDS seeks wider use of regulated assets.
Path to shops
DAI and USDS can be distributed or converted. But a processor supporting them does not create a company that owes holders regular money.
GENIUS Act
Likely not a payment stablecoin. Ambiguity comes from Sky's official 'protocol obligation' language and the law's broad definition of a person.
Latest
The move from DAI to USDS changes the economics, who controls it and its legal identity.
Can break by
Collateral losing its peg, governance takeover, an oracle or PSM failure, a custodian or SPV problem, or a contract migration error.
Limit
Swapping for USDC is not necessarily redemption for monetary value as the law defines it.
open: Whether the law treats the DAO or governance as an issuer or person, and which entity owns specific RWA claims.

items.title: Curve / Swiss Stake
items.text: Curve has no ordinary issuer, but the contract that mints crvUSD is easy to identify
kv: Owns
Curve DAO governs market-creating contracts (factories), markets, debt ceilings and fee routing. Swiss Stake is a development body, not a documented company that owes holders regular money.
Can say no
The DAO can change future markets, caps and fees. The contracts and templates set what can change after launch.
Makes money from
Admin fees on trading, lending and crvUSD interest, gauge rewards and vault revenue sharing. Swiss Stake also has proposed earnings from its interface.
Sits on
Stablecoin swap liquidity, crvUSD minting, and the peg and liquidation mechanisms
Legal entities
Curve DAO and its governance; Swiss Stake AG, where development, research, security and interface work is concentrated; token contracts; gauges; oracles; and Peg Keepers are separate actors.
Money products
crvUSD is a protocol debt asset, scrvUSD is a vault share and CRV is the governance and incentive token.
Control levers
ControllerFactory's power to mint, DAO votes, debt ceilings, fee-splitting contracts, oracles and liquidity rewards.
Depends on
Outside collateral, oracles and market liquidity, liquidators, governance and smart-contract security.
Stablecoin and DeFi role
A dollar created inside the protocol and a core source of liquidity. scrvUSD separates the base coin from savings that earn fees.
Path to shops
Likely converted into a payment coin a processor supports before it is spent.
GENIUS Act
Likely not a payment stablecoin, since no named company owes holders regular money. Whether the DAO or factory counts as issuer is open.
Latest
We found no regulator decision. Control is visible even where ordinary legal liability is not.
Can break by
An oracle or LLAMMA (Curve's soft-liquidation system) error, collateral crash, liquidity drain, hacked factory or governance, or smart-contract exploit.
Limit
Swiss Stake's development role does not make it liable for redemption.
open: Who the law treats as issuer or person, and how markets that cannot be changed after launch affect governance's liability.

items.title: Frax
items.sub: frxUSD live · licensing and who owes holders still in transition
items.text: Frax is trying to move issuance into a company while its DAO keeps control
kv: Owns
Frax DAO keeps the protocol's economics and the right to override. Frax Inc. PBC (public benefit corporation) takes on delegated compliance, reserve, bank-payment and issuer functions.
Can say no
The company issuer can enforce identity-check (KYC) and reserve policy. The DAO can revoke or override what it delegated. Custodians control their own mint and burn processes.
Makes money from
Income from reserves and collateral, protocol fees, DeFi strategies, and income the DAO controls.
Sits on
Issuance shared by a company and the DAO, DAO governance, bank minting and redemption, and collateral providers built into the protocol
Legal entities

Frax Inc. PBC—formerly FinresPBC—holds delegated issuer and compliance functions. Frax DAO keeps the economics and the power to revoke. Custodians and real-world-asset (RWA) providers built into the protocol, and interface entities, are separate.
Money products
frxUSD base coin, sfrxUSD wrapper, protocol collateral and partner-branded (white-label) layers.
Control levers
FIP (Frax Improvement Proposal) delegation, DAO override, issuer compliance, custodian choice, token administration and bank payment connections.
Depends on
Licenses, banks, custodians, providers of tokenized Treasurys and other RWAs, governance and trading venues.
Stablecoin and DeFi role
The clearest attempt to turn a protocol-created dollar into a coin under a regulated issuer's rules and owners.
Path to shops
Processors could accept it if the exact issuer, reserves and approval are certified. White-label coins may extend its reach.
GENIUS Act
A strong payment-stablecoin candidate, but not proven permitted. Rewards paid in the same token raise a yield question.
Latest
FIP-432 is a governance vote to delegate. It is not final approval or full proof of which entity legally owes holders.
Can break by
DAO–company conflict, losses at custodians or RWA providers, licensing failure, governance takeover, or strain on the wrapper or peg.
Limit
Evidence of a regulated pivot is not a finding of completed PPSI (permitted payment stablecoin issuer) status.
open: Who holds final legal authority after licensing, who owns the reserves, and whether the issuer or an affiliate pays rewards.

items.title: Liquity
items.sub: BOLD and LUSD live · core contracts cannot be changed
items.text: Liquity's core contracts have no administrator, so they cannot be paused or upgraded
kv: Owns
Liquity AG develops and supports the software. Core contracts that cannot be changed run borrowing, redemptions and liquidations, with no administrator who can upgrade them.
Can say no
The core design has no way to pause, upgrade, blacklist or move by governance vote. Front ends and third parties can still restrict access.
Makes money from
Borrower interest, gains from liquidations, Stability Pool returns and activity on third-party interfaces.
Sits on
Borrowing against more collateral than the loan, and redemption for crypto collateral
Legal entities

Liquity AG develops and supports software but does not run one official front end. Independent interfaces, the unchangeable contracts, and users and liquidators are separate. No named issuer that owes regular money is documented.
Money products
BOLD and LUSD are protocol debt assets. Stability Pool positions are separate.
Control levers
Core contract rules, collateral types fixed at launch, user positions, liquidators and independent interfaces.
Depends on
Ethereum, outside collateral and liquid staking token (LST) issuers, oracles and market liquidity, liquidators and front ends.
Stablecoin and DeFi role
A protocol dollar strongly built to resist censorship. It fits poorly with institutions' expectation that coins follow lawful orders.
Path to shops
Must be swapped on the market for a coin a processor supports.
GENIUS Act
Strong case that it falls outside the payment-stablecoin definition. Permitted-issuer compliance would need a successor system.
Latest
Any structural compliance change must come in new contracts or products, not a retrofit of the existing ones.
Can break by
Collateral, oracle or liquidity failure, chain disruption or interfaces disappearing. No administrator can step in to rescue it.
Limit
Unchangeable contracts do not remove sanctions, interface, collateral-issuer or market risk.
open: How the law treats unchangeable protocols, and practical distribution when intermediaries keep approved lists.

items.title: Ethena
items.sub: USDe and sUSDe live · USDtb partnership live
items.text: Ethena backs USDe with hedged crypto held by custodians, not a reserve account
kv: Owns
Ethena's protocol and operating entities coordinate USDe issuance, collateral custody, derivatives hedging and the sUSDe vault. Anchorage separately issues USDtb.
Can say no
Access for approved Mint Users, limits on minting and redemption, blocked staking addresses and operational risk controls.
Makes money from
Derivatives funding payments and basis (price-gap) income, staking and reserve income, paid out through sUSDe and ecosystem arrangements.
Sits on
Minting a synthetic dollar, hedging, holding collateral with custodians outside exchanges, and paying out yield
Legal entities

Ethena (BVI) Limited runs the application and the current USDe issuer relationship. Ethena OpCo Ltd., owned by Ethena Foundation, handles rewards, ENA distributions and sUSDe operations. 'Ethena Labs' provides research and communications. Anchorage Bank separately issues USDtb.
Money products
USDe (synthetic dollar), sUSDe (vault receipt) and USDtb (regulated reserve-backed coin) are separate.
Control levers
Mint User agreements, gatekeeper and blacklist roles, custody arrangements, how much goes to each trading venue, hedging operations, vault roles, ENA governance and Risk Committee powers.
Depends on
Centralized derivatives exchanges, market makers, Copper, Ceffu and other custodians, oracle data, stablecoin collateral and liquidity.
Stablecoin and DeFi role
A large synthetic dollar and yield product, and the brand partner for USDtb, which a federal bank issues.
Path to shops
USDe is generally converted to a payment coin or backs a card or wallet product. USDtb offers a more regulated base coin.
GENIUS Act
USDe does not neatly fit the GENIUS Act's narrow reserve and redemption rules. USDtb is analyzed with Anchorage as its issuer.
Latest
Its strength must be tested under real stress at exchanges or custodians, not only by normal attestations.
Can break by
Custodian or exchange default, hedges breaking down, funding rates reversing, collateral loss, or a mint-control or smart-contract failure.
Limit
Delta neutrality (hedging against price moves) is a risk-management claim, not a guarantee of redemption at par.
open: Ordinary holders' redemption rights, how concentrated the hedges are, treatment in bankruptcy and regulatory category.

items.title: Ondo
items.sub: USDY and OUSG live, limited to eligible investors
items.text: Ondo's tokenized Treasury products work like cash but legally remain securities
kv: Owns
Product issuers, adviser and general partner (GP) entities, token-control systems and distribution relationships for tokenized Treasury and fund products.
Can say no
Approved and blocked lists, pauses on buying in and redeeming, rate limits and controlled bridges. Agents and custodians keep their own controls over the assets.
Makes money from
Asset-management and advisory income, product income and spreads, and distribution and tokenization services.
Sits on
Issuing securities, deciding which investors qualify, controlling transfers, tokenized collateral and redemption
Legal entities

Ondo Finance Inc. runs services. Ondo Foundation is an independently governed Cayman foundation. Ondo Global Markets (BVI) Limited issues USDY today. Ondo I LP and its GP, and SEC-registered Ondo Capital Management, make up OUSG's structure.
Money products
USDY (a secured note), OUSG (a fund or limited-partnership interest) and their rebasing wrappers are securities, not payment stablecoins.
Control levers
Offering terms, OndoID (its identity check), transfer limits, custody and collateral agents, bridge controls and adviser decisions.
Depends on
Treasury and fund assets, Ankura and other agents, custodians, conversion through Circle and Coinbase, blockchains and eligible investors.
Stablecoin and DeFi role
Collateral that earns yield and a cash-management asset that can be swapped for stablecoins and used in DeFi (decentralized finance).
Path to shops
Normally converted into payment money first. Direct payment use is limited by securities eligibility rules and transfer controls.
GENIUS Act
The GENIUS Act excludes securities, so USDY and OUSG fall outside the payment-stablecoin definition.
Latest
Some product and blockchain integrations are live. Where descriptions of the issuer conflict, the current legal terms control.
Can break by
An issuer, agent or custodian problem, market loss, eligibility failure, bridge or control bug, or redemption delay.
Limit
A dollar-like net asset value (NAV) or instant conversion does not make the security a payment stablecoin.
open: How far tokenized securities can go into checkout, collateral and card products while keeping securities controls.

items.title: Morpho
items.sub: open lending markets anyone can create and curator-managed vaults live
items.text: Morpho's vault curators decide where lenders' money goes, doing the intermediary's job
kv: Owns

Morpho Association runs interfaces and ecosystem services. Morpho Labs is a separate development company. Control is split among governance and product-specific actors, across lending markets that cannot be changed and separately managed vaults.
Can say no
Governance cannot pause or rewrite existing Morpho markets. Vault owners, curators, allocators and sentinels can choose markets, allocate funds and use limited product powers.
Makes money from
Borrowing interest, curator and vault fees, protocol rewards, and income from interfaces and integrations.
Sits on
Lending markets anyone can create, how vault money is allocated, and which yields are chosen
Legal entities

Morpho Association is a French nonprofit association. Morpho Labs is a separate development company. Token governance, market creators and independent vault curators, allocators and sentinels are separate actors.
Money products
The underlying stablecoin is still owed by its issuer. The lender's or vault's receipt becomes a separate credit claim.
Control levers
Market settings, choice of price oracle, vault curation and allocation, caps, guardians and distribution through front ends.
Depends on
Stablecoin issuers, borrowers, collateral, price oracles, liquidators, curators and wallet and card distributors.
Stablecoin and DeFi role
A source of yield increasingly built into institutional wallets and Stripe/Privy-style products.
Path to shops
A card or wallet sells, borrows against or moves a Morpho position into spendable money before the merchant is paid.
GENIUS Act
A Morpho receipt or vault claim needs its own analysis. The base payment coin's issuer status does not protect the yield product.
Latest
Watch curator concentration and whether card and wallet integrations reach production.
Can break by
Bad debt, oracle failure, curator or allocation error, lack of liquidity, a flaw in a market that cannot be changed, a smart-contract exploit, or a front-end or custody failure.
Limit
Anyone can create a market, but that does not mean every vault is unmanaged or equally safe.
open: Which legal entity owes users in curated products, how bad debt is shared out and who controls emergency actions.

uncertain: The stablecoin competition is not one coin against another. Companies are racing to control the steps around the coin: legal liability to holders, reserves, ledgers, keys, risk, conversion to regular money and reaching customers.
Several statuses are the companies' own figures or plans ('figures are self-reported', 'some only announced'); each card says which.
The cards date from July 28, 2026; newer charter and product steps for some of the same firms are on the charters, issuers and freeze pages.
The other 11 cards of the same map are on the page 'What does each crypto company control, where can it stop a payment, and how does it make money?'

catalog_context.title: Which companies connect the new private money system
catalog_context.answer: No single coin or blockchain is taking over. Banks, crypto firms, card networks and market utilities each control a different step, and the most powerful firms may be the ones connecting those separate systems.

catalog_context.title: Who actually controls the crypto infrastructure
catalog_context.answer: Of 20 crypto networks and companies we track, only one is used at scale and none is proven under stress; many brands rest on a handful of legal providers.
